title: Reranking
story:
There are two ways to decide how well a document answers a query, and the difference between them is the entire reason this lesson exists.

The first encodes each text on its own and compares the results. The document's vector can be computed long before anybody asks anything, stored, and reused for every query forever. At query time you compute one vector and compare it against what is already there, which is arithmetic over numbers.

The second puts the query and the document through the model together and scores the pair. Nothing can be precomputed, because the computation depends on both halves, so every pair you want scored costs a full pass through the model.

The second is more accurate, and it is worth being precise about why rather than treating it as a mystery. A model that sees both texts at once can relate the parts of one to the parts of the other — the words of the question can be weighed against the words of the passage. A model that encodes the document alone has to commit to a single point in space before it knows what will be asked, so that point must be a summary that serves every possible question equally. One of these knows the question and the other does not, and everything else follows from that.

Now the cost, which Reimers and Gurevych measured in 2019 in a form that makes the decision obvious. Requiring both texts to go through the network together causes a massive computational overhead: finding the most similar pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences takes about 50 million inference computations, around 65 hours. Encoding each text independently and comparing the vectors brings the same task down to about 5 seconds, while maintaining accuracy.

Read those two numbers next to each other, because an architecture falls out of them. You cannot afford the accurate method over a corpus, and you can afford it over a handful. So do both. Use the cheap comparison across everything to produce a small candidate set, then spend the expensive joint scoring only on those candidates to put them in the right order. The first stage exists to not miss things; the second exists to sort what was found. That is reranking, and it is not a refinement bolted on afterwards — it is the only shape that fits the costs.

Which gives you the constraint that governs how you tune the whole thing. A reranker can only reorder what it was given. A document that never made it into the candidate set cannot be recovered by any amount of clever scoring, because the second stage never sees it. So the two stages are tuned for different things: the first for recall, meaning the right document is somewhere in the set it returns, and the second for precision, meaning the right document ends up at the top. Improving the scorer does nothing for a question whose answer was missed at stage one, and this is the most common way teams waste a month.

The size of the candidate set is the dial between them, and it is a dial you can measure rather than guess. The cost of the second stage is linear in how many candidates you pass it, and the chance the right document is in there rises as the set grows. Measure how often the correct passage appears in the first stage's output at a few different sizes, find where that curve flattens, and set the size just past the flattening. You now have a number with a reason attached, and a measurement you can repeat when either stage changes.

Two mistakes are worth naming because both are natural. The first is deciding the joint scorer is simply better and running it over everything — that is the version measured in hours rather than seconds, and it does not survive contact with a real corpus. The second is evaluating the scorer on its own, over the whole collection, when its actual job is conditional on what retrieval hands it. Measure the pair as a pipeline, on the questions you really get, or you are measuring something you do not run.

And since this stage sits inside the request path, treat it like any other dependency there: cap the candidate count, batch the scoring, put a timeout on it, and decide in advance what happens when the timeout fires. The sensible fallback is the order the first stage already produced, which is worse and perfectly serviceable — a slightly misordered answer beats a request that never returns.

problem.name: Two-stage retrieval
problem.shape: The accurate way to compare a query with a document costs a model pass per pair, and there are too many pairs.
tell: the right passage is in the results but not near the top
someone proposes scoring the whole corpus with the accurate model
the scorer is being evaluated over the full collection rather than over what retrieval returns
the candidate count was chosen without measuring how often the answer is inside it
problem.move: Retrieve cheaply over everything with precomputed vectors to build a small candidate set, then score those candidates jointly to order them. Tune the first stage for recall and the second for precision, and choose the candidate count by measuring where recall flattens.
problem.invariant: The second stage can only reorder the set the first stage returned, so end-to-end quality is bounded by the first stage's recall.
problem.breaks: Joint scoring cannot be precomputed, so its cost is linear in the candidates and lives in the request path — which rules out running it over a corpus and makes it a latency risk that needs a timeout and a fallback.

cost.time: one model pass per candidate, in the request path, growing linearly with the candidate count
cost.space: nothing can be cached between queries, since the score depends on the pair rather than on the document
cost.beats: vector comparison alone, which is fast and must summarise a document before the question is known, and joint scoring over everything, which is accurate and unaffordable

worked.problem: Why two stages rather than one, and what can a reranker not do?
worked.reasoning:
Because the accurate way to score is unaffordable over a corpus and perfectly affordable over a shortlist.

The two options differ in what can be precomputed. Encoding each text independently lets every document's vector be computed once, ahead of any question, and reused forever; at query time you encode one thing and compare. Putting the query and document through the model together depends on both halves, so nothing can be precomputed and every pair costs a full pass.

The joint version is more accurate for a reason worth stating: it can relate the parts of the query to the parts of the passage, while the independent version must commit the document to a single point before it knows what will be asked, so that point has to serve every possible question. One knows the question, the other does not.

The measured gap makes the design obvious. Reimers and Gurevych report that finding the most similar pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences takes about 50 million inference computations, roughly 65 hours, when both texts must go through the network together — and about 5 seconds when each is encoded independently and the vectors compared, while maintaining accuracy.

So: cheap comparison across everything to get a small candidate set, expensive joint scoring on those candidates to order them. Stage one exists to not miss things, stage two to sort what was found.

What a reranker cannot do is recover a document that never entered the candidate set — it only reorders what it was handed. That is why the stages are tuned for different targets: retrieval for recall, reranking for precision. Improving the scorer does nothing for a question whose answer was missed earlier, and that confusion wastes real months.

The candidate count is the dial, and it is measurable rather than a matter of taste: cost is linear in it, the chance the right passage is present rises with it, so I measure how often the correct passage appears in the first stage's output at several sizes and set it just past where that curve flattens.

The two mistakes I watch for are running the joint scorer over everything, which is the version measured in hours, and evaluating the scorer alone over the whole collection when its job is conditional on what retrieval passes it. And because this sits in the request path, I cap the count, batch the work, set a timeout, and fall back to the retrieval order, which is worse and entirely serviceable.

problem.practice: Take twenty real questions and record, for each, whether the correct passage appears in your retriever's top ten, top fifty and top two hundred. That table tells you both whether reranking can help you at all and how many candidates to pass it — and if the correct passage is often absent at two hundred, your problem is retrieval and no reranker will touch it.

beats.broke: The accurate comparison puts query and document through the model together, so nothing can be precomputed and the cost is a model pass for every pair — hours rather than seconds over a collection.
beats.fix: Use precomputed independent vectors to narrow the corpus to a short candidate list, then spend the joint scoring only on that list.
beats.cost: The reranker can only reorder what it was handed, so end-to-end quality is capped by the first stage's recall, and the scoring sits in the request path.

interview.q: Why two stages rather than one, and what can a reranker not do?
interview.trap: Tuning the reranker to fix misses. A document absent from the candidate set is unreachable — that is a recall problem at stage one, and no improvement to the scorer touches it.
interview.answer:
Because the accurate comparison is unaffordable over a corpus and cheap over a shortlist. Encoding each text independently lets every document's vector be computed once and reused forever, so a query is one encode plus arithmetic. Putting the pair through the model together depends on both halves, so nothing precomputes and every pair costs a full pass.

The joint version is more accurate because it can weigh the words of the question against the words of the passage, while the independent version has to commit the document to a single point before knowing what will be asked — a summary that must serve every possible question.

Reimers and Gurevych measured the gap in 2019: finding the most similar pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences takes about 50 million inference computations, roughly 65 hours, when both texts go through the network together, and about 5 seconds with independent encoding, while maintaining accuracy. The architecture falls straight out of those numbers — cheap retrieval over everything for a candidate set, expensive scoring over the candidates for order.

What a reranker cannot do is recover a document that never entered the candidate set. It only reorders what it was given, so the two stages are tuned for different things: retrieval for recall, reranking for precision, and end-to-end quality is capped by the first stage.

The candidate count is the dial, and I set it by measuring how often the right passage is present at several sizes and choosing just past where the curve flattens. Since the stage sits in the request path I also cap it, batch it, time it out, and fall back to the retrieval order — worse, and it returns.
